paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.heading: Kiosk assistant — Riverside Park
paragraphs.text: Cheerful person wanted to serve drinks and ice creams. No previous experience needed — full training given. Weekends only, April to September. Call in at the park office and ask for Mrs Dale.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.heading: Banqueting waiter/waitress — The Regent Hotel
paragraphs.text: Part-time evening work for experienced staff only. Excellent hourly rate plus tips, and a free meal on every shift. Two written references are essential. Telephone the events manager during office hours.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.heading: Family helper
paragraphs.text: Needed from March until the end of August to look after twin boys aged three. Patience and a sense of fun matter more to us than formal childcare certificates. Monday to Friday, 8 am – 5 pm. Must hold a driving licence. Please phone after 7 pm.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.heading: Early-morning cleaner
paragraphs.text: Busy medical centre on Mill Lane needs a reliable cleaner, 6 am – 8 am, Monday to Friday, so that all rooms are ready before the first patients arrive. £85 per week.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.heading: Office manager
paragraphs.text: Established curtain and upholstery firm supplying hotels and guest houses seeks a mature person with proven office experience. Afternoons only, 1 pm – 5 pm, Monday to Friday. Apply in writing to Ms R. Clarke.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.heading: Chef — The Lantern Bistro
paragraphs.text: Full-time chef for a lively new bistro opening in the town centre this spring. Salary and working hours open to discussion. Ring the owner, Tom Pascoe.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.heading: Café premises for lease
paragraphs.text: Fully equipped 40-cover café on the main coast road, available on a five-year lease. Would suit someone with long experience in the trade who now wants to be their own boss. Write to Box 118, Harbourside Weekly.

texts.title: Northern Star Overnight Coaches — Ticket Guide

paragraphs.text: Most of our tickets can be used on the overnight services between London and the north. A reclining-seat reservation costs an extra £12, except with Comfort and Pair tickets, which already include a reserved seat. Every overnight passenger receives a hot drink and a snack before arrival.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.heading: Early Bird
paragraphs.text: Our lowest fare: £39 return. Must be booked at least 21 days in advance and is valid only on coaches leaving after 11 am. No refunds unless we cancel the service.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.heading: Advance
paragraphs.text: £49 return when bought at least seven days before you travel. Refunds are possible, but a 20% handling fee is deducted.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.heading: Flexi Saver
paragraphs.text: £62 return. Can be bought up to the day of travel and used on any day except peak days: every Friday, 20–31 December and the Easter weekend. Departures between midnight and 3 am count as the previous day's departures.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.heading: Day Return
paragraphs.text: £70 return. On sale until departure, but valid only on coaches leaving between 9 am and midnight. Seats cannot be reserved.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.heading: Comfort
paragraphs.text: Enjoy one of our wider front-row seats. A return ticket with reserved seats in one or both directions; both reservations must be made when you book. Your stay must include a Saturday night. £110–£130.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.heading: Pair
paragraphs.text: A return package for two people travelling together, with reserved seats in one or both directions — a real saving for both of you. Both journeys must be booked at the same time. From £95.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.heading: Open
paragraphs.text: Our most expensive ticket, but it can be used on any coach at any time, right up to departure. Friday coaches are busy, so please arrive early.

paragraphs.text: Our clients visit our offices every day and rely on us for expert advice. The purpose of this policy is to ensure that all staff present a professional appearance that inspires confidence.

paragraphs.heading: General standards
paragraphs.text: A business suit is the standard for both men and women, although a smart jacket with suitable trousers or a skirt is also acceptable. Clothes must always be clean and ironed; anything torn or faded will not be accepted. Because no policy can cover every situation, staff are expected to use good judgement and to consult their line manager if they are unsure.

paragraphs.heading: Footwear
paragraphs.text: Smart shoes, boots and low-heeled shoes are all acceptable. Trainers and open sandals may not be worn in the office.

paragraphs.heading: Accessories
paragraphs.text: Ties, scarves and jewellery are welcome, provided they are discreet. Large or eye-catching items should be avoided.

paragraphs.heading: Fragrance
paragraphs.text: Please apply perfume and aftershave lightly. Some colleagues suffer from asthma, and strong scents can trigger breathing problems.

paragraphs.heading: Headwear
paragraphs.text: Caps and hats should not be worn indoors. Head coverings worn for religious reasons or as part of a cultural tradition are of course permitted.

paragraphs.heading: Casual Fridays
paragraphs.text: On selected Fridays, smart-casual clothing is allowed. Staff are encouraged to wear clothing that displays the company name. However, keep a jacket at your desk in case you need to meet a client.

paragraphs.heading: If the policy is not followed
paragraphs.text: A member of staff whose clothing does not meet the policy will first be asked not to wear the item again. If the problem continues, a written warning will be issued, and the employee may be sent home to change.
All salaries are reviewed every year, and increases reflect the performance of each individual employee. On top of your salary, you can enjoy the following benefits.

paragraphs.heading: Annual leave
paragraphs.text: All staff receive 25 days' paid leave a year, rising to 30 days after five years' service.

paragraphs.heading: Pension
paragraphs.text: Our company pension is open to all employees who have completed two years of service. The company pays the full contribution.

paragraphs.heading: Staff discount
paragraphs.text: After six months you will receive 15% off most items in our stores, rising to 20% after two years.

paragraphs.heading: Holiday cottages
paragraphs.text: The company owns several holiday cottages by the sea, which staff can rent at reduced prices.

paragraphs.heading: Theatre tickets
paragraphs.text: We pay half the price of theatre and cinema tickets for all staff.

paragraphs.heading: Learning fund
paragraphs.text: We offer generous support to staff who wish to take language courses or learn a new hobby, as well as those studying for professional qualifications.

paragraphs.heading: Financial support
paragraphs.text: Employees facing serious personal difficulties may apply for an interest-free loan.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the night of 12 March 1992, fire swept through Harlow Hall, a seventeenth-century manor house in the English Midlands. Roofers had spent the winter replacing old timbers, and their work was due to be finished on 15 March. The fire service arrived within twenty minutes, but the upper floor, with its library of rare books, could not be saved. On the ground floor, however, the situation was different. Staff, volunteers and neighbours formed long human chains and passed paintings, clocks and furniture out through the windows, so that almost 90 per cent of the ground-floor contents were rescued. That same night, a local hardware shop opened specially to supply the plastic sheeting that conservators needed to protect the rescued objects from the rain.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: By morning the hall was little more than a shell. Blackened beams hung from what remained of the walls, and the ground floor lay under several centimetres of ash and water. Visitors who had known the house described the scene as heartbreaking.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the weeks that followed, archaeologists and volunteers searched the ruins methodically. The site was first divided into numbered squares, and every fragment, however small, was photographed and its location noted. All the debris was then put into thousands of labelled sacks before being sieved and sorted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There were some surprising finds. A section of carved staircase thought to have been destroyed was discovered almost intact beneath a collapsed ceiling, and a set of eighteenth-century tiles was recovered from the cellar. The great tapestry from the hall had been taken down by firefighters only minutes before the roof gave way.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whether the hall should be rebuilt at all was hotly debated. Some argued that the money would be better spent elsewhere. In the end the owners, a heritage charity, decided to restore it, for three main reasons. First, much more of the original structure had survived than people had expected. Second, the house was fully insured, so the restoration would not have to be paid for from the charity's own funds. Finally, many of the rescued objects had been made specifically for the house and would lose much of their meaning if displayed anywhere else.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Finding people with the skills to do the work took many months. Every contract was put out to competitive tender, and firms were chosen only after their craftsmanship had been carefully assessed. The project brought a new generation of stonemasons and wood carvers to prominence, and several plasterers taught themselves techniques that had not been used for two hundred years — skills that are now in demand at other historic houses.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The restoration was completed in 1998, on schedule and within its £14 million budget, most of which was covered by insurance. The charity also took the opportunity to install a modern fire-detection system and to improve the heating and electrical wiring.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: When the hall reopened, many former staff were in tears as they walked through the rooms again. Visitor numbers in the first year were higher than ever before. Nevertheless, some critics still believe that a ruined house should have been left as a ruin, and the debate continues.
